title: Endocrine
rationale: Requested module. Adrenal is your highest-volume weakness at 56% over 27 questions, so this covers the adrenal axis properly and then the rest of the system — thyroid, calcium and diabetes emergencies — which have barely been tested.
objectives: Separate primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency using ACTH and the aldosterone/renin pair.
Predict the electrolyte and glucose direction of cortisol excess and deficiency in both directions.
Interpret thyroid function tests including the patterns that do not fit the simple feedback model.
Manage thyroid emergencies and state why the order of drugs matters in thyroid storm.
Work up hypercalcaemia by PTH, and treat hypercalcaemia of malignancy in the right order.
Distinguish DKA from HHS and apply the potassium rule before insulin.

sections.heading: The adrenal axis
sections.body:
Three layers, and **only two are ACTH-driven** — *salt, sugar, sex; the deeper you go the sweeter it gets*. Zona **glomerulosa** makes aldosterone under **RAAS control**; **fasciculata** makes cortisol under ACTH; **reticularis** makes androgens under ACTH.

| | Primary (Addison's) | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| ACTH | **High** | **Low** |
| Aldosterone | **Low** | Normal |
| Renin | **High** | Normal |
| Potassium | **High** | **Normal** |
| Pigmentation | Yes | No |

**Potassium is the discriminating electrolyte.** Hyponatraemia occurs in both — salt wasting in primary, loss of cortisol's suppression of ADH in both. Hyperkalaemia needs aldosterone gone, so it is primary only.

**Short Synacthen:** pass is roughly **>430 nmol/L at 30 min** (PathWest), with many labs using >450; older texts say 550. Assay-dependent, so a fair question gives you the range.

**Crisis:** IV/IM hydrocortisone 100 mg plus aggressive saline, immediately, without waiting for confirmatory results. **Fludrocortisone has no role acutely** — stress-dose hydrocortisone supplies ample mineralocorticoid activity.
sections.note: ACTH high means primary; hyperkalaemia occurs only in primary because it requires loss of aldosterone.

sections.heading: Aldosterone and renin — read renin first
sections.body:
**Aldosterone is high in both primary and secondary aldosteronism, so it carries no information on its own.**

| | Renin | Aldosterone | ARR |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary (Conn's)** | **Suppressed** | High | **High** |
| **Secondary** (renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis) | **High** | High | Normal |
| **Addison's** | High | **Low** | — |

In Conn's the adrenal secretes autonomously; the resulting volume expansion switches renin **off**. High renin means something upstream is driving the system.

Presentation: hypertension with hypokalaemia, often resistant. Confirm with the aldosterone/renin ratio after correcting potassium and, where possible, stopping interfering drugs. Then CT adrenals and **adrenal vein sampling** to distinguish a unilateral adenoma (adrenalectomy) from bilateral hyperplasia (spironolactone).
sections.note: Read renin first: suppressed means the adrenal is the problem, high means something upstream is driving it.

sections.heading: Thyroid — including the patterns that break the rule
sections.body:
| Pattern | TSH | Free T4 | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary hypothyroidism | **High** | Low | Gland failure |
| Subclinical hypothyroidism | High | Normal | Treat if TSH >10, symptomatic, pregnant, or antibody positive |
| Primary hyperthyroidism | **Low** | High | Graves', toxic nodule, thyroiditis |
| **Secondary hypothyroidism** | **Low or normal** | **Low** | **Pituitary** — the trap, because a low TSH looks like hyperthyroidism |
| Sick euthyroid | Low/normal | Low, low T3 | Non-thyroidal illness — do not treat |

**Graves' vs thyroiditis** decides management and the discriminator is uptake: **diffuse uptake in Graves', absent uptake in thyroiditis**, patchy in multinodular goitre, a hot nodule in toxic adenoma. TRAb confirms Graves'; eye disease and pretibial myxoedema are pathognomonic.

**Thyroid storm — order matters.** Give the **thionamide (propylthiouracil or carbimazole) BEFORE iodine**, because iodine given first provides substrate for further hormone synthesis. Then beta-blocker, corticosteroid (blocks T4→T3 conversion), and treat the precipitant.

**Amiodarone** causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism, and is worth remembering as a cause when the picture is otherwise puzzling.
sections.note: A low TSH with a LOW free T4 is pituitary disease, not hyperthyroidism.

sections.heading: Calcium — split by PTH
sections.body:
Measure **PTH** and the differential halves immediately.

**PTH high or inappropriately normal** → primary hyperparathyroidism (commonest outpatient cause; adenoma), tertiary hyperparathyroidism, familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (low urinary calcium — the one not to operate on).

**PTH suppressed** → **malignancy** (commonest inpatient cause): PTHrP from squamous tumours, bone metastases, or myeloma. Also vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease, thyrotoxicosis, immobilisation.

**Hypercalcaemia of malignancy — the order is the answer:** aggressive **IV 0.9% saline rehydration first** (these patients are profoundly dry from polyuria), **then IV bisphosphonate** (zoledronic acid; takes 2–4 days). Denosumab where renal function precludes it. **Never fluid-restrict.**

Symptoms: *stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychic moans*, plus polyuria and dehydration.
sections.note: PTH splits hypercalcaemia in two: high means parathyroid, suppressed means malignancy until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Diabetic emergencies
sections.body:
| | DKA | HHS |
|---|---|---|
| Typical | Type 1, hours | Type 2, days |
| Glucose | >11 | Often >30 |
| Ketones | **High** | Minimal |
| pH / bicarbonate | **Acidotic** | Near normal |
| Osmolality | Variable | **Very high** |

**The potassium rule governs both.** Total body potassium is depleted even when the serum level looks normal or high, because acidosis has driven it extracellularly. **Insulin drives it back in.** If potassium is **below 3.5, replace it before starting insulin** — otherwise you precipitate fatal hypokalaemia.

Other points: fluids first and generously; **bicarbonate is not routine** even with marked acidosis; look for the precipitant (infection, missed insulin, MI, new diagnosis); and in HHS correct osmolality **slowly** to avoid cerebral oedema, with a lower fluid and insulin rate than DKA.
sections.note: In DKA, replace potassium before starting insulin if it is below 3.5 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has fatigue and weight gain. TSH is 11.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) and free T4 is 8 pmol/L (10-20).
questions.explanation: High TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism — the gland has failed and the pituitary is driving hard. Subclinical would have a high TSH with a normal free T4. Secondary would have a low or normal TSH with a low T4, because the pituitary is the problem.
questions.point: Primary hypothyroidism gives a high TSH with a low free T4.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has a corrected calcium of 2.95 mmol/L (2.20-2.60). PTH is 8.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9).
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A raised calcium with an inappropriately high PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism — normally hypercalcaemia should suppress PTH completely. In malignancy PTH is suppressed, because the driver is PTHrP or bone destruction rather than the parathyroid. PTH is the first test and it splits the differential in half.
questions.point: Hypercalcaemia with a high or inappropriately normal PTH indicates primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has glucose 26 mmol/L, pH 7.14, bicarbonate 9, ketones 5.6, and potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2).
questions.lead: What is the correct first step?
options: IV fluids and potassium replacement before insulin
questions.explanation: Potassium is low. Insulin drives potassium intracellularly and will precipitate dangerous hypokalaemia — so fluids and potassium come first, with insulin typically withheld until K⁺ ≥3.5 or run alongside replacement. Bicarbonate is not routine in DKA even at this pH; it worsens paradoxical CNS acidosis.
questions.point: In DKA with potassium below 3.5, replace potassium before starting insulin.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has resistant hypertension on three agents and K 2.9 mmol/L. Aldosterone is elevated and plasma renin activity is suppressed.
questions.lead: What is the diagnosis and next step?
options: Primary aldosteronism; CT adrenals and consider adrenal vein sampling
questions.explanation: High aldosterone with suppressed renin and a high ratio is primary aldosteronism — the adrenal is autonomous, and the resulting volume expansion switches renin off. Secondary aldosteronism has high renin driving high aldosterone with a normal ratio. Next steps are CT adrenals and adrenal vein sampling to separate a unilateral adenoma (surgical) from bilateral hyperplasia (spironolactone).
questions.point: Primary aldosteronism has suppressed renin; secondary aldosteronism has high renin driving the aldosterone.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has weight loss, palpitations and heat intolerance. TSH is suppressed, free T4 elevated. Radioiodine uptake scan shows absent uptake throughout the gland.
questions.explanation: Absent uptake means the gland is not making hormone — it is leaking preformed hormone from inflammation, which is thyroiditis. Graves' gives diffuse uptake, multinodular goitre patchy uptake, and a toxic adenoma a single hot nodule. This matters because thyroiditis is treated symptomatically with a beta-blocker and is self-limiting, whereas antithyroid drugs are useless against a gland that is not synthesising.
questions.point: Absent radioiodine uptake in thyrotoxicosis indicates thyroiditis, which leaks preformed hormone rather than synthesising it.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is confused and polyuric. Corrected calcium is 3.4 mmol/L. She is clinically dehydrated.
questions.lead: What is the correct sequence of treatment?
options: IV 0.9% saline rehydration, then IV bisphosphonate
questions.explanation: Rehydrate first. Hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and profound dehydration, and saline both restores volume and promotes calciuresis. Then give an IV bisphosphonate, which takes 2-4 days to act. Giving the bisphosphonate to a dehydrated patient risks nephrotoxicity and does nothing for the immediate problem. Fluid restriction is exactly wrong.
questions.point: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is rehydrated with IV saline before a bisphosphonate is given.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on amiodarone has TSH 0.02 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 34 pmol/L (10-20). He is thyrotoxic.
options: Amiodarone causes hypothyroidism but not hyperthyroidism
Amiodarone can cause both hypo- and hyperthyroidism, and the cause here needs distinguishing
This must be Graves' disease coincidentally
The TSH is unreliable on amiodarone and should be ignored
questions.explanation: Amiodarone is roughly 37% iodine by weight and causes both hypothyroidism and thyrotoxicosis. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis has two types: type 1, excess synthesis in an abnormal gland (treated with thionamides), and type 2, a destructive thyroiditis (treated with corticosteroids). Distinguishing them changes treatment, and they can coexist. This is a common cause of a puzzling thyroid picture.
questions.point: Amiodarone causes both hypothyroidism and thyrotoxicosis, and thyrotoxicosis has synthetic and destructive types needing different treatment.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has fatigue and amenorrhoea. TSH is 0.3 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) and free T4 is 7 pmol/L (10-20). She has also had reduced libido and postural dizziness.
questions.lead: What does this thyroid pattern indicate?
questions.explanation: A low TSH with a LOW free T4 breaks the usual feedback logic — a failing gland should drive TSH up. Both being low means the pituitary is not producing TSH: secondary hypothyroidism. The amenorrhoea, reduced libido and postural symptoms suggest other pituitary axes are failing too, so assess the whole pituitary and image it. Critically, replace corticosteroid BEFORE thyroxine — giving thyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis by raising metabolic demand.
questions.point: A low TSH with a low free T4 indicates pituitary failure, and corticosteroid must be replaced before thyroxine.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with untreated Graves' disease develops fever 39.5°C, agitation, atrial fibrillation and vomiting after an emergency appendicectomy.
questions.lead: Which sequence of drug administration is correct?
options: Iodine first, then propylthiouracil, then beta-blocker
Propylthiouracil first, then iodine at least an hour later, plus beta-blocker and corticosteroid
questions.explanation: Thyroid storm. The thionamide must be given before iodine: iodine blocks hormone release, but given first it also supplies substrate for further synthesis. Propylthiouracil is preferred over carbimazole here because it additionally blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion. Add a beta-blocker (propranolol, also blocking conversion) and a corticosteroid, and treat the precipitant — here surgery and possibly infection.
questions.point: In thyroid storm the thionamide is given before iodine, because iodine given first supplies substrate for further hormone synthesis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops proximal weakness, oedema and hypertension over 6 weeks. He is not cushingoid in appearance. K 2.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 33, glucose 12.4.
options: Aldosterone excess from an adrenal adenoma
Very high cortisol saturating 11β-HSD2 and acting on mineralocorticoid receptors
questions.explanation: Ectopic ACTH produces extremely high cortisol, which overwhelms 11β-HSD2 — the renal enzyme that normally inactivates cortisol — so cortisol spills onto mineralocorticoid receptors, causing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Hyperglycaemia follows from cortisol's insulin antagonism. The rapid course explains the absent Cushingoid habitus: weakness, oedema and hypertension dominate instead. Note this is the exact inverse of the Addisonian pattern.
questions.point: Ectopic ACTH causes hypokalaemic alkalosis because very high cortisol saturates 11-beta-HSD2 and acts on mineralocorticoid receptors.
